To "get to grips with" something means to make a serious effort to understand, deal with, or take control of something that is difficult, unfamiliar, or challenging.

When you "get to grips with" something, you stop avoiding it or feeling confused by it, and instead you engage with it directly and tackle it properly.

Think of it this way: if something is hard to understand or handle, and you finally sit down, put in effort, and start making sense of it — that is exactly what this idiom describes.

The word "grip" literally means to hold something tightly and firmly with your hand. Picture someone grabbing a rope, a tool, or an opponent in a wrestling match — they have a firm, controlled hold on it.

The idiom is rooted in this physical image. Just like a wrestler needs to get a firm grip on their opponent to gain control, we use the same idea for mental and practical challenges. When you "get to grips with" a difficult problem, you are metaphorically grabbing hold of it firmly instead of letting it slip away from you.

This is why the idiom carries a sense of active effort and control — it's not passive. You are the one reaching out, grabbing the problem, and wrestling with it.
The Full Breakdown of What It Implies

When someone says they need to "get to grips with" something, it usually implies three things at once:

1. There is difficulty involved.
The thing in question is not easy. It is complex, new, overwhelming, or unfamiliar. You wouldn't say you need to "get to grips with" tying your shoelaces — that's too simple.

2. An effort must be made.
The phrase suggests that you need to invest real time, focus, and energy. It's not something that happens automatically.

3. The goal is understanding or control.
The end result of "getting to grips with" something is that you understand it properly, or you are able to handle it effectively. You go from being lost or overwhelmed to being in command.

Here are examples across different situations so you can see how naturally this idiom fits into real life:

Learning something new:
"I have just started learning Python. It's taking me a while to get to grips with all the syntax."

A new job or responsibility:
"She has just been promoted to manager. She needs to get to grips with the new role quickly."

A difficult subject:
"Many students find it hard to get to grips with quantum physics."

A complex situation:
"The government is struggling to get to grips with the housing crisis."

A new piece of technology:
"My grandfather finally got to grips with his new smartphone after a few weeks of practice."

An emotional challenge:
"After losing his job, it took him some time to get to grips with his new reality."

Notice how in every single example, there is something difficult, new, or overwhelming, and the person is working to understand or handle it properly.
"Get to Grips With" vs. "Come to Grips With"

You will often hear both versions, and they are very close in meaning. Here is the subtle difference:

"Get to grips with" is more commonly used when talking about understanding or practically dealing with something — a skill, a task, a concept, a system.

"I need to get to grips with this new accounting software."

"Come to grips with" is more commonly used when talking about emotionally accepting a difficult truth or reality — a loss, a hard fact, a painful situation.

"She is still coming to grips with the death of her father."

That said, in everyday conversation, many native speakers use them interchangeably, and you will rarely be misunderstood either way.

Here are other idioms and phrases with a similar meaning, so you can recognise them when you encounter them:

"Get a handle on" — to begin to understand or control something.
"I'm trying to get a handle on my finances."

"Wrap your head around" — to fully understand something difficult or strange.
"I can't wrap my head around this theory."

"Come to terms with" — to accept something difficult emotionally.
"He came to terms with his illness."

"Grapple with" — to struggle to deal with or understand something.
"She is grappling with a tough decision."

All of these share the spirit of struggling with something hard and working through it, just like "get to grips with."
Register: When and Where Is It Used?

This idiom is completely natural in both formal and informal settings. You can use it in:

  • Everyday conversation with friends and colleagues
  • Professional emails and reports
  • News articles and academic writing
  • Speeches and presentations

It is most common in British English, but it is well understood and used in all varieties of English worldwide.

It is important to understand a few things this idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean you have already mastered something. "Getting to grips with" is the process, not the finished achievement.
  • It does not carry a negative judgement. Saying someone needs to "get to grips with" something is not an insult — it simply means there is a challenge they need to work through.
  • It does not mean a quick or instant thing. It usually implies a period of effort and adjustment.

Core meaningTo seriously try to understand, deal with, or take control of something difficult
ToneNeutral; works in formal and informal contexts
OriginFrom the physical idea of gripping something firmly to gain control

Close relative"Come to grips with" (more emotional); "get a handle on" (very similar)
One Final Way to Remember It

Imagine someone handed you a large, slippery, awkward box. At first, you fumble with it — your hands keep slipping, you can't hold it properly. Then, after some effort, you get a firm grip on it and carry it with confidence.

That fumbling-then-gripping moment is exactly what "getting to grips with" something feels like — you go from confusion and struggle to confidence and control.
